## 1. Identity summary

Peramanathan Sathyamoorthy is a Senior Software Engineer with over nine years of professional work on web products, public APIs, integrations and developer tooling, mostly in TypeScript, JavaScript, React and Node.js, with Python and Rust in production and open-source work. He holds an MSc in Computer Science from Uppsala University and an MSc in Operations Research and Computer Applications from NIT Tiruchirappalli, and he has two peer-reviewed papers on energy-efficient data communication for the mobile Internet of Things.

From April 2017 to December 2024 he worked at Oneflow AB in Stockholm, a digital signature and contract management platform. He started as a JavaScript Developer, built the Integration Team as a Full Stack Integration Engineer, led the engineering team as Engineering Team Lead, and returned to hands-on work as Senior Software Engineer for a TypeScript migration and permissions work.

Since December 2024 his role has been Independent AI/SI product and systems engineering (agentic workflows). In that time he shipped:

- adaptate, a TypeScript validation library on npm (adaptate, @adaptate/core, @adaptate/utils, latest 2.4.2, each release published with SLSA provenance). It turns one Zod or OpenAPI schema into per-screen views and validates streaming LLM tool-call JSON while it is still arriving.
- kanithanj.ai, a product that helps people find roles they can grow into, from true facts and evidence. Its desktop app (collab-finder) is a Tauri, Rust and React app with a SQLite ledger; 1.0.0 shipped on 19 August 2026 and 1.3.0 on 23 November 2026.
- Ensembly, a Rust operator kernel that lets several agent harnesses share one ledger, one memory sync and one approval flow.
- A marketplace of agent plugins and a skills library that load into Grok Build, Cursor and Claude Code.
- A Next.js portfolio and CV pipeline that renders the site, the PDF CV and these agent files from one data source.

Much of his deep-learning and systems work is private and not public. The public repositories are a record that grew slowly as he learned and crafted over time, not the full depth of that work.

What sets him apart is the set of habits he brings to a team:

- He designs for cost and evidence first. His 2015 research argued that systems stay viable only when the cost of the next useful observation falls while the quality of decisions rises. He now applies the same rule to LLM agents: tokens, context and memory are costs to earn back.
- He builds tools that save time and compound, from a Babel plugin for translations in 2017 to plugins that run his daily engineering work in 2026.
- He prefers verification by tooling over verification by memory: tests that run README examples, provenance on every release, and scripts that flag risky changes.

## 5. Shipped work, in technical depth

### 5.1 adaptate: typed, validated data from any schema or stream

Links: https://github.com/p10ns11y/adaptate · https://adaptate-site.vercel.app · npm: adaptate, @adaptate/core, @adaptate/utils

Timeline: first commit 2 November 2024 (f506830). First npm publish of adaptate on 4 November 2024. Version 2.4.2 of all three packages published on 24 November 2026 with SLSA provenance (predicate https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1). npm downloads from 25 October to 23 November 2026: @adaptate/core 1,092, @adaptate/utils 987, adaptate 864 (npm counts include CI and bots).

The problem. One data model is used by many screens and services, but each one needs different fields to be present. Teams usually copy the schema per consumer, and the copies drift. In the LLM era there is a second problem: a model streams a tool call as JSON, and `JSON.parse` throws until the last byte arrives, so the UI shows nothing.

The design.

- One schema, many views. `transformSchema(schema, config)` in @adaptate/core takes one Zod schema and a config object that says which fields a consumer needs (`true` required, `false` optional, nested objects, `{"*": config}` for every array item). It returns a Zod schema with the same inferred type. `satisfies Config<T>` turns a misspelled key into a type error. `makeConditionalSchemaTransformer` adds rules such as `requiredIf`.
- OpenAPI interop. `openAPISchemaToZod` and `zodToOpenAPISchema` in @adaptate/utils convert both ways and keep `required`. `getDereferencedOpenAPIDocument` loads a spec from the filesystem or a URL and resolves `$ref`s.
- Streaming validation. `createAgUiPartialValidator` reads AG-UI `TOOL_CALL_ARGS` deltas and returns the partial value so far, typed from the schema, plus per-view readiness. `createStreamValidator(...).final()` reports which screens are ready when the call ends. `validateStructuredOutput` accepts TanStack AI style output. `createFrameThrottle` emits at most once per animation frame.
- Incremental parsing. `@adaptate/core/stream-incremental` keeps its place in the stream, so each character is read once. `fromAsyncIterable` and `fromAsyncIterableSteps` take strings or bytes from any async iterable (Node `Readable`, Web `ReadableStream`). On a 966-character sample, the incremental feed made 966 character visits; re-parsing the growing buffer made 68,304. Property tests assert that visits equal the text length.
- Result API for choke points. `parse`, `parseAsync` and `parseStream` from `@adaptate/core/result` return a `Result` with an ok track and an error track instead of throwing. `parseStream` checks each partial value against an optional partial schema and the closed value against the full schema. The "choke point" idea: guard the few boundaries where outside data enters (an API response, a queue message, an AI/SI model's tool call), and let the rest of the app trust the checked value.
- Standard Schema interop, so Valibot and ArkType schemas work through `@adaptate/core/standard`, and an optional Effect subpath.

Hard problems solved.

- Deep and hostile input. The resolver and both converters walk with loops, not recursion. Tests run them on documents 100,000 levels deep, and the partial JSON reader returns the leaf of a 100,000-level document with the last character missing. A `$ref` chain past depth 500 throws `RangeError`, and a circular schema throws `RangeError` instead of running out of memory.
- Proof for every claim. A proof page maps each README sentence to a test, a script or a CI job, and the README snippets run as tests.
- Performance budgets. CI compares each pull request with its base and fails if a timed case is more than 5% slower.
- Type packaging. CI checks the packed tarballs on TypeScript 7 and 6 for `bundler`, `node16` and `nodenext` resolution.
- Supply chain. Releases are published from CI with SLSA provenance.

Its roots are in the Zod validation library he built at Oneflow in 2021–2022, according to his CV.

### 5.2 kanithanj.ai and collab-finder: roles you can grow into

Links: https://kanithanj-ai.vercel.app · https://github.com/p10ns11y/collab-finder · walkthrough https://captain.kingsparrow.space/shipped/collab-finder

Timeline: first commit 4 June 2026 (aac535a). Tags v1.0.0 on 19 August 2026, v1.1.0 on 8 September, v1.2.0 on 22 October, v1.3.0 on 23 November 2026. About 300 commits.

What it is. kanithanj.ai is a product that helps a person narrow down which roles they can grow into, using true facts and evidence about themselves and about each company. The desktop app is built with Tauri v2, Rust and React, and the public site runs on Vercel.

Architecture.

- A Rust backend (`src-tauri`) with modules for the SQLite ledger (`db.rs`), decisions (`decide.rs`), LLM routing (`llm_route.rs`), the xAI client (`xai.rs`), live X search (`x_search.rs`, `x_query.rs`), the Swedish public job board (`platsbanken.rs`), firm durability (`firm_durability.rs`), rank configuration (`rank_config.rs`), a local network graph (`network_graph.rs`), secrets in the OS keyring (`secrets.rs`) and a pulse module (`pulse.rs`).
- A React front end with screens for discovery, pipeline, an X search view and preferences, and a command palette.
- A CV tool (kanithanj.cv) builds a role-specific CV packet locally from one `cvdata.json` file, so the CV facts never fork.

Design decisions.

- The model is the cheap part. Cost, fit, rate limits and a human promote step decide what happens. The model is called only when the signal is worth the spend.
- Human approval only where it matters. The user steps in when a guard fires (fit, cost, rate, promoting a CV), not on every step.
- Personal data stays on disk. The local network graph and the ledger never leave the machine. API keys live in the OS keyring.
- Quality checks in CI: build, domain checks and `cargo test`, plus mutation testing with Stryker.

### 5.3 Ensembly: one ledger, one memory sync and one approval flow under many agent harnesses

Links: https://github.com/thecuriousts/ensembly · essays https://captain.kingsparrow.space/articles

Timeline: rebuilt from 13 July 2026 (4f35ce1) as a Rust workspace. Tag v0.2.0 on 13 July 2026. The record layer landed on 18 November 2026 (30fd7b3, "scalable append log, keys sidecar, envelope v2 bus", PR #97).

What it is. A thin operator kernel that sits under capture harnesses such as Grok Bot, Grok Build, Cursor and Claude Code. The rule: bots and harnesses propose, Ensembly authorises, claims and completes. One SQLite writer owns the ledger.

Architecture. Rust crates `ensembly-kernel`, `ensembly-memory`, `ensembly-schema`, `ensembly-agents`, `ensembly-bundle`, `ensembly-paths`, plus `evalbench-core` and `evalbench-cli` (a synthetic-data evaluation bench) and `retrieval-bench`. An MCP server (`ensembly-mcp`) and a one-command installer for each harness (`install.sh --harness cli|cursor|claude|grok`). Episodic memory uses CRDTs and never decides. A pulse-pack syncs memory between hosts.

Hard problems.

- Several agents writing to one state without conflicts: one writer, durable authorise/claim/complete states, idempotent retries ("dedupe exact retries", PR #91).
- Memory retrieval measured before it is trusted: a retrieval benchmark (PR #93), full-text search recall checks (PR #95) and an honest index measurement (PR #99).
- Clock trust across machines: a clock offset sampler (PR #96) with cancel on timeout (PR #98).
- A stranger test: `scripts/stranger-test.sh` installs into a temporary HOME with synthetic data and runs the full test suite, so the install works for someone who is not the author.

### 5.4 Agent plugins marketplace

Link: https://github.com/p10ns11y/plugins (first commit 15 July 2026, about 200 commits)

One repository serves as a plugin marketplace for Grok Build, Claude Code and Cursor. Each plugin bundles skills, slash commands, agents and hooks, and some ship Rhai workflows for Grok Build. Selected plugins:

- pulse-memory (29 August 2026): "Pulse instead of dump." An admissions filter for agent recall. It keeps sparse, dated and sourced snippets, resolves contradictions instead of averaging them, and keeps SQLite as the store.
- live-engine (8 November 2026): an action runner with one live working set, few specialists, verify before irreversible acts, then recover.
- eva-emptiness (1 August 2026): a blank-sheet harness (Prior, Probe, Simulate, Score, Act or Ask) with a shell tether that asks on an ordinary `git push` and denies force-push.
- mission-map (15 August 2026): critical path, PERT and Monte Carlo kernels in C and a Rust graph, for planning work under uncertainty.
- intelli-route and trust-stack (26 September 2026): route one goal to at most four skills, and place each invariant at its earliest layer (shape, check, watch, skill, then a human guide).
- pstack-map (31 August 2026) and aihero-map: map other public skill stacks onto his own without copying them, with credit.
- craft: specifier, coder, cleaner, hardener and QA roles, with CRAP scores on touched functions and mutation testing.
- layout-content-view: checks layout, content and view stability for web pages.

### 5.5 Agent skills library

Link: https://github.com/p10ns11y/skills (first commit 8 June 2026)

About 60 skills, each a `SKILL.md` that agents load by name and description. In the README's words: "Most agent failures are not model failures. They are context, coordination, and guardrail failures." Skills cover token-efficient context, safe parallel agents with git worktrees, supply-chain hardening, splitting work into reviewable PRs, BDD strategy, MVU refactors, semantic HTML and CSS, and a formal dialect (AppGenMathPhyLang) for precise specs.

### 5.6 devprofile: portfolio, CV pipeline and agent profile

Links: https://captain.kingsparrow.space · https://github.com/p10ns11y/devprofile

Timeline: first commit 8 September 2025 (478b92c, "Simple landing page, cv, cvdata"). About 420 commits.

Built with Next.js 16 App Router, React 19 and TypeScript, shadcn/ui and Radix UI, React-PDF for the CV, local embeddings with @huggingface/transformers for a profile Q&A, Biome, and Playwright end-to-end tests. One `cvdata.json` drives the landing page, the CV page, the PDF and the `/api/cv/data` endpoint, so content cannot drift. The articles carry their own Open Graph images. The site will serve `/llms.txt` and `/agents.md` as plain text for crawlers and agents.

### 5.7 imm: independent module maintainer

Link: https://github.com/p10ns11y/imm (first commit 22 September 2026, Rust)

A supply-chain idea he first described on X on 21 May 2026. Install a direct dependency as its whole source, and do not install the packages under it. Every other use is kept as an extract: the function you call, a hash of the original bytes, an audit, and a diff if an agent changed the code. The binary never runs package code, and `approve --approver agent` exits with an error, so an agent cannot approve its own extract.

### 5.8 proposales-planner-bench

Links: https://proposales-planner-bench.vercel.app · https://github.com/p10ns11y/proposales-planner-bench (first commit 6 October 2026)

One sentence in, ranked venues back. A Next.js app on the Proposales API that validates API readers with @adaptate/utils and finds gaps in a brief with @adaptate/core. It uses the Vercel AI SDK with xAI, AG-UI, shadcn/ui and Playwright. The repository reads in a fixed order: front page, actualization, product, architecture, work log, steering.

### 5.9 thepulimaangani: Tamil prosody in the browser

Links: https://github.com/p10ns11y/thepulimaangani · walkthrough https://captain.kingsparrow.space/shipped/thepulimaangani

First commit 9 April 2020, a Rust and React app. Today it is a Rust parser for Tamil prosody (யாப்பு), compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-pack, with a TanStack Start React UI. The analysis runs in the browser with no backend.

### 5.10 Smaller tools that show the pattern

- babel-plugin-react-intl-messages-generator (first commit 13 January 2017, npm 15 January 2017): reads JSX and generates `defineMessages` files, so a whole React project gets translation keys without hand work.
- hy (2 November 2021, npm @p10ns11y/hy): a git wrapper that takes a phrase such as "rebase then push", prints each step and runs it.
- graphite-merge-rebase-squash-evaluation-test (September 2024): compares merge strategies by how each one affects commit signatures.
- prototype-it-to-explain-itself (June 2026): the smallest complete prototypes, so the code explains the idea: LLM and ReAct agents, diffusion, computer vision, NLP.
- agent-prompt-tuning-lab (June 2026): turns Cursor agent transcripts into prompt-tuning datasets, skills and rules, with privacy filtering first.

| 28 Aug 2026 | Archive is not memory: data, context, fact and memory are four different things; memory is a trace kept because it should change a later action | https://x.com/Peramanathan/status/2093296586675912712 , essay https://captain.kingsparrow.space/articles/memory-issue/archive-not-memory |
| 2 Oct 2026 | A decision model is not a smaller chat model; agreement between two models is not verification; check correlation with Cohen's kappa | https://x.com/Peramanathan/status/2106128083027664952 |
| 7 Oct 2026 | Review areas, not diffs: split the app into areas from its imports, set each area's review cadence from git churn, keep PR review for secrets, auth, dependencies, payments and personal data | https://x.com/Peramanathan/status/2107917582926025047 |
| 8 Nov 2026 | Body-inspired agent design: an organ exists only when no other can own the function; one shared bus; flow follows demand; compute cannot exceed intake | https://x.com/Peramanathan/status/2119436174641050037 |
| 16 Nov 2026 | AI/SI bots are the new browsers: build light services that run inside bot ecosystems, start opt-in, log everything, act freely only on safe and reversible artifacts | https://x.com/Peramanathan/status/2122431792619855888 |

The two strongest early threads:

1. Measure less, decide better (2014 to 2026). His thesis and his 2015 and 2017 papers argued for selective sensing: learn which signals matter, then report less while decisions improve. Ten years later the same rule shapes his agent work. Context and memory cost tokens, latency and energy, so an agent should load only what can change the next decision. The line runs through the thesis repository (2014), the CloudCom paper (2015), the journal paper (2017), the EEaaS essay (August 2026) and the pulse-memory plugin (August 2026).
2. Tooling that enforces the rule, so people do not have to remember it (2017 to 2026). The Babel plugin generated translation files instead of asking developers to write them. The TypeScript conversion script kept history instead of asking reviewers to trust a rewrite. adaptate's README examples run as tests. imm refuses agent self-approval in code. The eva-emptiness tether denies force-push in a hook.

## 7. Ideas still ahead

These are directions he has written about and started building. The industry has not settled on them yet.

- Pulse memory as a decision qualifier. Frontier products mostly treat memory as more context. His position (X, 8 November 2026) is that memory is a past trace kept because it should change a later action: "a qualifier for the next decision, not a larger window." The harness emits a compact pulse with a key, a verification flag and a prefetch hint, and memory returns only a snippet that still matches its locked revision. Proof: https://x.com/Peramanathan/status/2119434548081516763 and the pulse-memory plugin.
- The Ensembly record layer. Every fact has one owner, every write carries an idempotency key, events keep event time and versions in an append-only log, and every action follows "write intent, act, verify". Views only read. Proof: Ensembly PR #97 (18 November 2026) and the retrieval benchmarks.
- Runtime verification of what enters a system. adaptate's choke-point Result API is the first step: validate at the boundary and keep an ok track and an error track. The next step, tracked as an open issue in adaptate, is to check a download's hash and metadata before it is stored, and to bring formal checks into everyday runtime code. imm applies the same idea to dependencies.
- Decision models beside LLMs. Use a calibrated classifier over a closed set of labels on the hot path, use the LLM when the label set might be wrong, and measure agreement with Cohen's kappa before trusting a second judge.
- Area-based review for AI/SI-written code. PRs land faster than people can read them, so the unit of review becomes the system's area, on a cadence set by churn, with PR review kept for security-critical changes.
- Light services inside bots. Services that run inside a user's bot, opt in per run, log and replay everything, and never act on anything irreversible without a consent card.

## 8. Work style and thinking process, 2010 to now

### 8.1 How his thinking changed, era by era

Research era, 2010 to 2016 (Uppsala University, Bumbee Labs internship)

- Focus: energy-constrained systems, measurement cost, distributed systems, peer-to-peer computing, algorithms. His best-graded courses at Uppsala were Advanced Algorithms, Algorithms and Data Structures II, Peer-to-Peer Computing and Cryptology.
- Thinking: measuring is itself a cost. Learn which signals matter, then measure less.
- Evidence: thesis repository (9 October 2014), CloudCom 2015 paper, a Wiley journal paper (2017), MongoDB aggregation for footfall analytics at Bumbee Labs (2015), and Coursera data-science course projects with public repositories (March 2015).
- On X in 2012 he shared Fred Brooks' "Plan to throw one away" (20 February 2012) and Knuth on sorting and searching (22 January 2012), early signs of the prototype-first habit he still follows.

Product-builder era, 2016 to 2017 (Weavler)

- Focus: accessibility, small-team full-stack delivery, cost.
- Thinking: when a task repeats across a codebase, write the tool once. When users differ, adapt the interface to them (text customisation, colour filters, speech).
- Evidence: the Babel plugin on npm (January 2017); reactube (February 2016), a React app built to explain its own `props` and `state`; comment-on-highlight (February 2017), with no third-party packages.

Integration and platform era, 2017 to 2021 (Oneflow, JavaScript Developer and Integration Engineer)

- Focus: legacy modernisation without stopping the product, public APIs, other companies' permission models.
- Thinking: grow the new system inside the old one (React Router inside Backbone). Evaluate before adopting: he built small evaluation repositories before committing, such as ckeditor5-tour (January 2018), react-redux-quest (March 2018), formik-react-select-testing (February 2020) and draftjs-editor-app (April 2021, before co-leading the rich-text editor). Teach what you know: a lightning-talk repository on git (September 2020).
- Rust and WebAssembly from 2020: rust-wasm-app and rust-wasm-bindgen-app (April 2020), the start of thepulimaangani.

Leadership and quality era, 2021 to 2024 (Oneflow, Team Lead and Senior Engineer)

- Focus: team practices, test strategy, type safety, permissions.
- Thinking: turn the team's real habits into tooling (mob-testing sessions became the first Playwright tests). Migrate in place and keep history. Put one owner on each rule (one ACL module).
- Evidence: CV entries for these roles; bestjs, a test framework built from Jest packages (October 2021); hy (November 2021); merge-strategy evaluation (September 2024); latex-cv (October 2024); adaptate (November 2024).

Agent era, 2025 to now — Independent AI/SI product and systems engineering (agentic workflows)

- Focus: LLM tooling, agents, memory, verification, supply chain.
- Thinking: code is now cheap and evidence is the expensive part (X, 1 October 2026). People own intent, acceptance criteria and release, and agents do the rest. Every irreversible act is verified first. Memory must be earned, not dumped.
- Evidence: devprofile (September 2025), the skills library (June 2026), collab-finder (June 2026), the plugins marketplace (July 2026), Ensembly (July 2026), the essays (August and September 2026), imm (September 2026), area-based review (October 2026) and adaptate streaming and Result APIs (November 2026).

### 8.2 Traits, each as a contribution to any team

Each trait has a dated, public example.

1. Builds tools that compound and save the team's time. Example: a Babel plugin that generated translation files for a whole React project (January 2017); a script that converted JavaScript to TypeScript and kept history (Oneflow, 2023–2024, per CV); plugins and skills that run his engineering workflow (2026). What a team gets: repeated work becomes a one-time tool.
2. Goes deep, then builds on the depth. Example: adaptate went from a dynamic schema builder (November 2024) to OpenAPI round-trips, streaming validation, an incremental parser and a Result API (November 2026), with 214 commits and every README claim tied to a test. What a team gets: a component that keeps getting better instead of being rewritten.
3. Security by design, with no back doors. Example: his X posts on device back doors and spyware (25 January and 29 March 2026); keys in the OS keyring in collab-finder; SLSA provenance on every adaptate release; imm refusing agent self-approval; a supply-chain warning during the 2026 npm worm outbreak (12 May 2026). What a team gets: security decisions made in the design, not patched later.
4. Rules enforced by tooling, not by memory. Example: performance budgets that fail a PR more than 5% slower; README snippets run as tests; a shell tether that denies force-push; CRAP limits and mutation testing (X, 1 May 2026). What a team gets: fewer review arguments, because the check runs on every change.
5. Verifies before irreversible acts. Example: the live-engine plugin's rule "verify before irreversible acts, then recover" (8 November 2026); "write intent, act, verify" in the Ensembly record layer; "Own and act freely only on the own artifacts and data that are safe and reversible" (X, 16 November 2026). What a team gets: agents and automation that stay safe to run.
6. Reviews by area and risk, not by habit. Example: "review areas, not diffs" (X, 7 October 2026), with nightly, weekly or monthly cadence by churn and PR review kept for secrets, auth, dependencies, payments and personal data. What a team gets: review effort spent where the risk is.
7. Lean, visual documentation. Example: repositories that read in a fixed order with a Mermaid map (proposales-planner-bench), proof tables (adaptate), and essays built around diagrams. What a team gets: docs a new person can follow in minutes.
8. Measures before trusting. Example: Ensembly's retrieval benchmark ("measure only") before any ranking change; Cohen's kappa before trusting a second model (X, 2 October 2026); a stranger test for installs. What a team gets: decisions based on numbers from the team's own cases.
9. Credits other people's work. Example: adaptate's inspiration page credits Dan Abramov's essays; pstack-map and aihero-map credit Lauren Tan and Matt Pocock without copying their work; his X post on supporting open-source authors (6 July 2026). What a team gets: a good citizen in open-source and inside the company.
10. Explains by building the smallest working thing. Example: reactube, a React app that explains its own props and state (February 2016), and prototype-it-to-explain-itself (June 2026). What a team gets: ideas tested in code before they turn into long documents.

### 8.3 Gaps in this record

- Much of his deep-learning and systems work is private and not public. The public repositories are a record that grew slowly as he learned and crafted over time, not the full depth of that work.
- Public evidence from 2017 to 2024 is thinner than from 2025 on, because most of that work was in a closed-source codebase. Oneflow outcomes and percentages come from his CV and were not checked against outside sources.
- His X posts from 2011 to 2024 are mostly personal and general. Technical posting starts in earnest in late 2024.
- No public talks or conference recordings were found apart from the 2020 git lightning-talk repository and the 2015 conference paper.

## 9. How skills and plugins help the work

He treats agent instructions as engineering artifacts: versioned, tested, credited and shared.

- Skills hold procedures that are boring, tedious, error-prone or heavy on memory. In his words (X, 23 May 2026): "these are skills sometimes boring, tedious, error-prone and need high cognitive load to do them manually." He says a small set of them "pretty much solves 90% of the problem in any arbitrary projects."
- Plugins bundle skills with commands, agents and hooks, so one install works across Grok Build, Claude Code and Cursor. The marketplace catalogs live in one repository.
- Hooks enforce the rules a person would forget: ask before `git push`, deny force-push, stop when an approval belongs to a human.
- Memory plugins keep agent context small and verified: pulse-memory admits only dated, sourced snippets that should change a later action.
- Routing plugins keep each task to a few skills (intelli-route allows at most four) and put each check at its earliest layer (trust-stack).
- Planning plugins compute the critical path and uncertainty (mission-map uses PERT and Monte Carlo), so work follows the chain that decides the outcome.
- Results he has posted: about 20 PRs in two days of 20 to 60 minute bursts, driven from a phone, with "great foundations, security guards, tests, CRAP limit" (X, 1 May 2026).

## 10. Working methods

- Plan in hours and ship in small, reviewable PRs. Large changes are split with a dedicated skill.
- Intent, acceptance criteria and release stay with people; agents do the rest.
- Every public claim maps to a test, a script, a CI job or a link.
- One source of truth for data. The CV, site, PDF and agent files all render from one file.
- Verify before anything irreversible: merges, releases, payments, deletions and messages.
- Supply-chain hygiene: pinned package managers, pnpm workspace policies, Socket Firewall, and SLSA provenance on releases.
- Accessibility and semantic HTML by default.
- Credit inspiration in the docs, in the same style for every source.

Senior Fullstack Engineer and Product Engineer, Stockholm. 9+ years in TypeScript, JavaScript, React, Next.js and Node.js, plus Python and Rust. At Oneflow (2017–2024) built the Integration Team, ran the public API and CRM integrations (HubSpot, Salesforce, Dynamics), led the team, set up Playwright end-to-end testing and led a TypeScript migration. Since December 2024, in Independent AI/SI product and systems engineering (agentic workflows): maintainer of adaptate on npm (Zod, OpenAPI, streaming LLM tool-call validation; 2.4.2 with SLSA provenance), builder of kanithanj.ai (Tauri, Rust, React, SQLite) and Ensembly (Rust agent kernel), and author of agent plugins and skills for Grok Build, Cursor and Claude Code. Strengths: LLM tooling, agents, context and memory design, evals, CI/CD, supply-chain security, accessibility. MSc Computer Science, Uppsala University; two IoT papers.
